name: Backerganj cyclone (1584)
region: Bakerganj coast (Barisal and Patuakhali), present-day Bangladesh
headline: A five-hour storm described in Mughal-era chronicles drowned the coast of Bakla (Bakerganj); only well-built temples were said to survive.
numbers: Low: compilation figure without a traceable contemporary count
timeline: A cyclone and storm surge strike the Bakla/Bakerganj coast of Bengal.

What happened: The storm is known from Mughal-era sources, notably the Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl and the later Riyaz-us-Salatin, later summarised in British district gazetteers. They describe a storm lasting about five hours with thunder and a sea that overwhelmed the coast, destroying houses and boats; only Hindu temples with strong foundations were spared.
The death toll and why it is uncertain: The chronicles give about 200,000 deaths. There was no census, the area's population is unknown, and chronicle numbers of this period are often rounded or rhetorical. Lists even disagree on the year (1582 or 1584). The event is real; the number is a historical estimate to be treated with caution.
Why it matters: It shows that the north-eastern Bay of Bengal has produced catastrophic surges for as long as there are records: the shallow shelf, funnel-shaped coast and low delta that made 1876, 1970 and 1991 so deadly were already in place.
